title: We Are South Maui: Community Plan Advisory Committee Meeting of January 25th (fixed)

issues.title: Using recycled R1 water for irrigation and firefighting

recap.headline: South Maui plan committee adopts four watershed policies, stalls on gulch setbacks
recap.in_60_seconds: The South Maui Community Plan Advisory Committee met to work through the plan's mauka-to-mākaʻi watershed management policies, with the County Public Works Director on hand as a resource. Ten people testified, mostly asking for stronger "require" language, better links to mauka lands and the Southwest Maui Watershed Plan, axis deer control, and less concrete in drainage plans. The committee adopted policies 2.4.1 through 2.4.4 without objection, including a reworded wetland buffer policy. It did not reach a motion on 2.4.5, the 100-foot gulch setback, after debate over which gulches it covers, and recessed to continue next week. Members also leaned toward adding an extra weeknight meeting to catch up, since the committee is behind schedule.

parts.title: Opening, roll call and introductions
presented: Meeting opened at 5:30 p.m. with quorum.
A committee member who is a developer described past projects, including a 161-unit project for the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands.
Planning staff introduced a new planning department leader with about 20 years of planning experience who will attend meetings.

parts.title: Live streaming news and how to speed up meetings
presented: Meetings stream on Facebook for now; Akaka live streaming is expected to start around the middle of next month.
The committee is behind: all 17 transportation actions, 5 policies and 16 actions in another section, all 15 water policies and 17 actions, and 11 historic stewardship policies and 6 actions remain.
Proposals: take one topic at a time, read materials in advance, ask testifiers only clarifying questions, and keep speaker discussion on the community plan.
Another option is a second weekly meeting or a longer schedule, as another community plan committee did.

next.what: Meetings begin live streaming through Akaka
next.when: around the middle of next month

parts.title: Public testimony, part 1
presented: The Public Works Director introduced himself as a resource to help the committee work through the document.
Testimony was limited to three minutes per person on the watershed management goals and policies.

raised.concern: Policy 2.4.1 should reference the County wetlands ordinance, Ordinance 5421, and drop or define the "federal nexus" wording, which changes with federal rules.
Use "require" or "shall" instead of "encourage" or "support" for buffers, erosion control and avoiding water quality impacts (2.4.6, 2.4.7, 2.4.8).
The plan should connect to mauka lands, by implementing and updating the Southwest Maui Watershed Plan and forming a working group with Kula residents.
Add "natural infrastructure" to definitions and strategies, and fix the map legend to show gulches.
Green waste dumped into drainages adds to flooding; a public education program could help.
Axis deer are stripping mauka land, sending soil to the reef; support deer fencing, riparian restoration and native plants.
Make more use of recycled R-1 and reclaimed water, including on the landscape and for public restrooms.
The drainage master plan update should place drainage basins mauka of the urban growth boundary where possible.
Protect, restore and acquire wetlands, keep Māʻalaea mauka areas in open space, and add wetlands to policy 2.4.12; some landowners want to sell or donate wetland parcels.
Hybrid or virtual meetings would let more people take part.
The gulch definition and map treat small drainage ways like deep gulches; a universal 100-foot setback is too broad and could be tied to 100-year flows over 1,000 cubic feet per second instead.
The Kīhei drainage master plan relies too much on concrete; the Eco Solutions alternatives and permaculture-style approaches have not been incorporated.
Gulches need adequate buffers, and policies should respect the cultural view of surface and underground water flows.
South Maui needs a water conservation goal and plan; hotels are allowed far more water per acre than on Oʻahu.

parts.title: Committee questions for Public Works and Planning
presented: The Kīhei drainage master plan is a high-level flood study estimated at about $200 million before COVID, covering flooding only.
The County has no dedicated drainage funding; Public Works is looking at federal infrastructure money and Natural Resources Conservation Service programs.
Staff is short, and even if work started today, a project would be about six years out.
Planning staff said a wetlands map required by the new ordinance is due this year; flood rules follow FEMA floodplain maps.

answered.said: The wetlands ordinance is in effect and a required wetlands map is being bid and is due this year; whether building on wetlands is allowed depends on the property.
The drainage master plan was finalized, and the Eco Solutions alternatives will be posted as an appendix; the plan is a starting point, not final design.
Kūlanihākoʻi Gulch carries too much water for a mauka basin, so its channel must be cleared; smaller flows could be diverted into mauka basins, as the master plan contemplates.
Public Works is open to ideas like a regional stormwater park, but worries whether ecological solutions hold up in big floods and who maintains them.
Public Works is shifting from flood control toward water quality and watershed management, and rerouted flows can be looked at.
What to do about South Kīhei Road and sea level rise, including managed retreat, is still unanswered.

next.what: Final drainage master plan posted on the Public Works website

parts.title: Adopting watershed policies 2.4.1 to 2.4.4
presented: 2.4.1 reworded to preserve wetlands with buffers that mitigate pollutants, support ecosystems, allow migration and plan for future sea level rise.
2.4.2 kept as written, with a definition of nature-based solutions to be added.
2.4.3 trimmed to support restoration of degraded wetlands and connected systems and their buffers.
2.4.4 kept as written, requiring low impact techniques for new development and redevelopment.

answered.said: Policies should state their intent plainly; 2.4.1 is about buffers around wetlands, and defining wetlands with traditional knowledge could be a separate policy.
Nature-based solutions cost more to maintain, so requiring them everywhere, including affordable housing, should be weighed carefully.

parts.title: Policy 2.4.5 gulch setbacks
presented: Draft keeps mapped gulches in open space with no new permanent structures within 100 feet of the top of the bank, unless low impact design is used.
The 100-foot setback came from the West Maui plan and is common on the mainland.
No motion was made; members said they need to review the map first.

answered.said: Suggested saying "natural drainage ways", using 100-year flood limits or 100 feet from the top of the bank, and dropping the open space term and the low impact exception.
Current drainage standards already bar buildings within the 100-year flood limits of natural drainage ways.
The Kīhei drainage master plan maps all gulches mauka to mākaʻi and can help sort large from small ones.
Open space can be preserved in several ways, such as a conservation easement, without changing a parcel's zoning.

next.what: Members review the gulch map before deciding on 2.4.5

parts.title: Extra meetings and recess
presented: A member proposed long Saturday meetings to catch up; others preferred an extra weeknight at the usual time.
A show of hands found more support for an extra weeknight than a Saturday.
The meeting was recessed, so the next session continues on 2.4.5 without new testimony.

answered.said: Permanent structures in 2.4.5 should not include infrastructure; he will attend or send written suggestions if he cannot.

next.what: Meeting resumes where it left off, without new public testimony
Online form sent to schedule an extra weeknight meeting

bills.name: Ordinance 5421
bills.what: The County wetlands ordinance that defines wetlands more broadly than federal rules and sets rules and buffers for development.

bills.name: Southwest Maui Watershed Plan
bills.what: A watershed plan that connects mauka lands with South Maui and that testifiers want the community plan to implement.

bills.name: Maui Island Plan
bills.what: The island-wide plan mentioned as dividing watershed planning by district.

bills.name: Kīhei Drainage Master Plan
bills.what: A County flood study sizing drainage needs and mapping gulches through Kīhei, estimated at about $200 million.

bills.name: South Maui Community Plan
bills.what: The community plan the committee is revising, including its watershed management policies 2.4.1 to 2.4.5.

bills.name: West Maui Community Plan
bills.what: The plan that already uses a 100-foot gulch setback, cited as a model.

votes.what: Policy 2.4.1 reworded: preserve wetlands with buffers that mitigate pollutants, support ecosystems, allow migration and plan for sea level rise
Policy 2.4.2 as written, adding a definition of nature-based solutions
Policy 2.4.3 trimmed to support restoring degraded wetlands, connected systems and their buffers
Policy 2.4.4 as written, requiring low impact techniques in development

open_questions.question: Which gulches would the 100-foot setback in policy 2.4.5 apply to, and should smaller drainage ways be treated differently?
Is development still allowed on wetlands, and where are wetlands mauka of the highway?
How will the County pay for and staff Kīhei drainage projects, with no dedicated drainage funding?
What will happen to South Kīhei Road as sea level rises?

moments.quote: I want to support the protection and rehabilitation of riparian zones with ferro-angular fencing and native plants. Our gulch is our riparian zones, our streams are our Malpita-Makai connections.
moments.about: A new conservation nonprofit working with the mauka ranches backed the plan's watershed policies, pointing to deer fencing and native planting along gulches.

moments.quote: Our proposals for creating a wetlands map. The wetlands ordinance requires a map to be prepared this year, and so we are working on that.
moments.about: Planning staff said the county is reviewing proposals for a wetlands map, required by the new wetlands ordinance, that bears on the plan's wetland policies.

moments.who: Director of the Department of Public Works
moments.quote: Thank you. So the James Master Plan was finalized. The alternatives prepared by Equal Solutions will also be posted as an appendix.
moments.about: The Public Works director told the South Maui plan advisory committee that the Kīhei drainage master plan is final and that the less concrete-focused alternatives will only be added as an appendix.

moments.who: Director of the Department of Public Works
moments.quote: And it's going to be expensive and it's going to take a lot of time to get the plans, get the land, get the permitting, all of that coordinated. Even if we started today, talking six years out to get something built.
moments.about: The director warned that Kīhei flood control projects tied to the plan have no dedicated funding and would take at least six years to build.
